Planify — smart planning for students

Planify helps students and teams quickly organize tasks, track progress, and review monthly results in a clean, accessible interface

What it is

An online planner for creating and saving daily, weekly, and monthly plans with clear progress tracking

The problem

Many students lose track of tasks, miss deadlines, and cannot easily review their progress

Why it matters

A good plan saves time, improves focus, and helps students reach study goals more reliably

What makes it special

Simplicity, monthly summaries, and account support make Planify a practical tool for everyday planning.

Project overview

Planify is a web app for creating plans where users can build a daily, weekly, or monthly schedule, save it to a personal account, and review results at the end of each period

  • What it is: a planner for tasks and study routines
  • The problem it solves: lack of structure and control over task completion
  • Why this matters: it helps users stay organized and improve productivity
  • What makes it unique: quick setup, easy registration, and clear monthly summaries

Features

Step 1. Create a plan

Choose the period, list tasks, and set priorities to build a structured schedule

Step 2. Register account

Save plans to a personal profile so you can access them from any device

Step 3. Review results

Monthly summaries show completed tasks and areas that need more attention

Step 4. Clear design

A white and gold palette keeps the interface calm, modern, and easy to use

Usage

1. Open planify site

Feedback Evidence

Throughout development we collected feedback from our sponsor and real users at each stage to guide improvements.

Alpha Sponsor Interview — Aliaskar

At the Alpha stage, Aibar presented the current state of Planify to the sponsor Aliaskar — walking him through the core features: task scheduling, quick tasks, habits with streak tracking, and the daily progress percentage. The video interview covered the following key points:

Topic: What are you planning to add next?

We explained that the next planned features were global long-term goals — allowing users to set big yearly or monthly ambitions — and a more developed progress tracking system to visualize how users move toward those goals over time.

Sponsor concern: Mobile experience feels less comfortable

Aliaskar noted that using Planify on a mobile device was noticeably less convenient than on desktop — the layout did not adapt well to smaller screens. We acknowledged this and committed to improving mobile responsiveness in future versions.

✓ Key recommendation from sponsor

Aliaskar's main suggestion was to add a short onboarding instruction inside the app — a simple guide that explains to new users how the planner works and where to start. He felt that without any hint or tutorial, first-time users might feel lost. This was valuable feedback as it pointed to a real usability gap we had not considered.

Summary of Alpha feedback

  • The core planning features (tasks, habits, schedule) were well received
  • Sponsor wanted to see bigger goal-setting features added in future versions
  • Mobile layout needs to be improved for smaller screens
  • A built-in usage instruction or onboarding guide should be added for new users

Version Timeline

Planify evolved through three stages — each version added new capabilities based on real feedback and testing.

Alpha First working version

The Alpha version introduced the core planning features. Users could add tasks, mark them as done, plan their day by hour, and see a live progress percentage showing how much of the day was completed. Habit tracking with streaks and targets was also included from the start.

Day Schedule

Quick Tasks

Habits Tracker

Beta Accounts added + UI improvements

The Beta version introduced user accounts — users could now register, log in, and log out. The UI was also significantly polished with cleaner layouts and better spacing. However, at this stage accounts only worked on a single device; logging in from another device was not yet supported.

Login Page

Day Schedule (logged in)

Quick Tasks (logged in)

Habits (logged in)

Final Cross-device accounts via Firebase

The Final version solved the cross-device problem using Firebase as the backend. Users can now log in to the same account from any phone, tablet, or computer and see all their tasks and habits synced in real time. The interface remained clean and familiar from Beta, with the key upgrade being fully working cloud authentication and data persistence.

Evidence of Development

Here is an overview of the tools and technologies used to build Planify, and how the project progressed from idea to final product.

Tools used

  • HTML & CSS — page structure and styling
  • JavaScript — interactivity and logic
  • Firebase — user authentication and cloud data storage
  • GitHub & VS Code — version control and code editing
  • GitHub Pages — publishing the live site

Key development changes

  • Alpha → Beta: added login/register system, improved UI layout
  • Beta → Final: replaced local storage with Firebase so accounts work across all devices
  • Added 4-stat dashboard (Tasks Today, Completed, Progress %, Habit Streak)
  • Habit tracker with streak counter and target days

Before vs After — Account system

Before (Alpha/Beta): Tasks and habits were saved in the browser's local storage. This meant data was only available on the device where it was created — logging in on another phone showed an empty account.
After (Final): Firebase Authentication and Firestore replaced local storage entirely. Data now syncs to the cloud, so users can access their full account from any device instantly.

Final Reflection

Looking back at the full development journey — from the first Alpha build to the finished product — here is an honest assessment of what changed, what worked, and what comes next.

What improved the most from Alpha to Final?

Without question, the biggest leap was in functionality. The Alpha version was a solid prototype — tasks, habits, and a day schedule all worked — but everything lived only in the browser. There was no memory between sessions, no accounts, and no way to pick up where you left off on a different device. By the Final version, Planify became a real product: users can create an account, log in from their phone or laptop, and find all their data exactly as they left it. That shift from a local tool to a cloud-connected app is what transformed Planify from a school project into something genuinely usable.

What feedback was most useful?

Two pieces of feedback shaped the project the most. First, the sponsor pointed out that without accounts, any progress a user made would disappear — making the app hard to trust or rely on. That pushed us to prioritize Firebase authentication in the Beta stage. Second, user testing revealed that the interface in early builds felt slightly cramped and hard to read on smaller screens. Acting on that feedback led to the cleaner, more spacious layout seen in the Final version, where stats are clearly separated, tabs are easy to tap, and the overall flow feels much more intuitive.

What would we still improve?

Planify currently focuses on daily and quick tasks, which is a strong foundation — but there is clear room to grow. The most natural next step would be adding a monthly and yearly goal system, where users can set a big goal (like "learn a new language" or "run 100km") and have it broken down into weekly and daily steps automatically. A built-in calendar view would also make planning feel more visual and connected. Finally, a progress history page — showing completed weeks and months — would let users actually see how far they have come, which is one of the most motivating things a planner can offer.

Sponsor Interview

Aibar: Hi Aliaskar, thank you for being the sponsor for Planify. To start, could you tell us about your background and your interest in supporting a project focused on goal setting and scheduling?
Aliaskar: I’ve spent a lot of time managing different tasks, and I’ve seen how easy it is for people to lose track of long term goals when they get overwhelmed by daily chores. I’m interested in supporting student projects that solve real-world productivity gaps using clean, functional tech.
Aibar: We noticed that many people make daily lists but forget their yearly ambitions. Why do you think this disconnect is a problem worth solving?
Aliaskar: It’s a major issue because without a big picture, daily tasks feel like a treadmill. People burn out because they don't see progress toward their actual life goals. It’s a community problem; if students or professionals can't plan, they can't reach their full potential.
Aibar: What would make Planify worth your support? What impact should it have on a user to make you proud of the project?
Aliaskar: I’d be proud if a user told me they finally finished a yearly goal, like learning a language or a new skill, because the app broke it down into daily steps. It needs to promote intentional living rather than just busy work
Aibar: We are targeting students and young professionals. Who do you think would benefit most from this daily to yearly system?
Aliaskar: Definitely students in intense programs or early career professionals. They need to gain the skill of prioritization. The app shouldn't just list tasks; it should help them decide what is actually important for their future.
Aibar: In an app like Planify, what are the must have features for you, and what should we avoid?
Aliaskar: A must have is a visual link between a daily task and a larger goal. If I’m doing a workout today, I want to see how it contributes to my yearly health goal. Avoid feature creep, don't add too many buttons or social media sharing. Keep it focused and minimalistic.
Aibar: Since this is a student project, do you have any concerns about our scope or the technical difficulty of building this?
Aliaskar: My main concern is the data structure. Linking yearly, monthly, and daily data can get messy. I suggest you focus on a very solid Daily and Weekly core first. Ensure the progress journal reflects how you handle these technical hurdles.
Aibar: Finally, what is the one thing that would convince you to fully support Planify, and what advice would you give us before we start coding?
\Aliaskar: I’ll support it if the UI is clean and it actually works without bugs. My advice: Start small. Build a perfect daily planner first, then expand to the yearly view. If the foundation is weak, the rest won't matter.
